Quantile of Means: A Bonus-Free Ensemble Method for Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning

Asaf Cassel Affiliation: Google Research Email: asafca@google.com    Aviv Rosenberg Affiliation: Google Research Email: avivros@google.com
Abstract

Optimal Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms typically rely on carefully constructed count-based uncertainty estimates to drive exploration. Although theoretically sound, such estimates are hard to compute in practical settings and therefore offer limited insight for designing exploration heuristics. Meanwhile, ensembling has emerged as a practical approach, but remains without theoretical justification. Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, we propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Our simple count-free approach achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, providing theoretical grounding for ensemble-based exploration in RL.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a general framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, where an agent interacts with an environment to optimize a long-term objective. RL algorithms have achieved remarkable success across domains ranging from robotics and games (Mnih et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017; Haarnoja et al., 2018) to Large Language Models (LLMs; Stiennon et al. (2020); Ouyang et al. (2022)). Despite this progress, designing algorithms that can efficiently explore their environment – gathering informative experience while avoiding excessive trial and error – remains one of the fundamental challenges in RL.

Efficient exploration is central to achieving optimal performance in RL. In principle, optimal algorithms rely on carefully constructed uncertainty estimates to balance exploration and exploitation. Count-based approaches, in particular, offer a theoretically elegant means of quantifying uncertainty, leading to algorithms with near-optimal regret guarantees. However, these methods depend on explicit access to state-action visitation counts or precise transition models – quantities that are infeasible to compute or approximate in high-dimensional or continuous environments. Consequently, while these methods yield important theoretical insights, they provide limited guidance for practical exploration strategies.

In contrast, ensemble-based methods have become a staple of modern deep reinforcement learning (Lee et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021). By maintaining a collection of function approximators and leveraging their diversity to drive exploration, ensemble methods have achieved empirical success across a wide range of domains (Osband et al., 2016a; Osband et al., 2016b; Pathak et al., 2019; Peer et al., 2021). Yet, despite their practical utility, the theoretical basis for their effectiveness remains poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear how or why ensembling induces the kind of optimism or uncertainty quantification required for efficient exploration.

Recent progress in Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB) has begun to bridge this gap. In Cassel et al. (2025), a simple batch ensemble scheme was shown to achieve variance-dependent regret bounds for stochastic bandits – matching the performance of carefully tuned count-based methods – without requiring knowledge of the reward distributions or explicit confidence bounds. This result demonstrates that ensemble diversity alone can serve as a proxy for uncertainty, providing a count-free, distribution-agnostic route to optimal exploration in the bandit setting.

While Viel et al. (2025) recently adapted the bandit ensemble technique of Cassel et al. (2025) to MDPs in an imitation learning context, their approach achieves suboptimal rates and requires binarizing the state space – a construction that scales quadratically with the state space and cannot be applied heuristically in a function approximation setting. This leaves open the question of whether a direct ensemble method, without such structural modifications, can achieve optimal regret in MDPs.

In this work, we answer this question affirmatively. We propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon MDPs that selects actions according to a fixed quantile of an ensemble of Q-value estimates. This simple mechanism naturally captures optimism in the face of uncertainty, while requiring no explicit counts, no posterior computation, and no prior knowledge of reward distributions.

Contributions.
  1. 1.

    Instance-optimal regret for MDPs. We prove that our algorithm achieves instance-optimal (variance-dependent) regret bounds for tabular finite-horizon MDPs, matching the best known results (Zanette and Brunskill, 2019; Zhou et al., 2023) – previously attainable only through complex count-based bonus constructions. To our knowledge, this is the first provably efficient ensemble-based exploration algorithm for MDPs, and moreover it achieves optimal rates.

  2. 2.

    Optimal bandit bounds via quantiles. The quantile-based approach also yields improved results in the bandit setting, shaving a logarithmic factor from the regret of Cassel et al. (2025) and achieving the optimal instance-dependent rate. See analysis in Appendix C.

  3. 3.

    Distribution-agnostic algorithm, distribution-adaptive analysis. Our algorithm encodes no distributional assumptions – it works unchanged for bounded, sub-Gaussian, and non-negative heavy-tailed reward distributions. Yet the analysis can leverage the true concentration properties of the underlying distributions (e.g., KL-based bounds for Bernoulli rewards), yielding tighter guarantees without algorithmic modification.

  4. 4.

    Simple and transparent analysis. We present the complete proof in the main paper. The absence of bonus terms makes the key arguments – particularly the replacement of empirical value functions with optimal ones for establishing optimism – considerably more transparent than in prior variance-dependent analyses.

Extending ensemble-based exploration from bandits to MDPs is substantially more challenging than a per-state reduction: Q-value estimates at each step depend on subsequent value estimates through Bellman backups, breaking the independence structure that makes the bandit analysis clean. Standard covering arguments over the value function address this dependence but result in an ensemble size linear in the number of states, rather than logarithmic. Achieving optimal dependence requires more careful arguments that replace the empirical value function with the optimal one when establishing optimism – a technique that, in prior work, is always intertwined with intricate bonus constructions (Zanette and Brunskill, 2019; Zhou et al., 2023). In our setting, the absence of bonuses makes this argument considerably more transparent, suggesting that ensemble methods may be a more natural algorithmic primitive for exploration in MDPs than the bonus-based paradigm. Whether this approach extends to linear or general function approximation settings remains an interesting open question.

1.1 Related work.

Variance-dependent regret in MDPs. Achieving minimax optimal regret in tabular MDPs has been the focus of a long line of work (Azar et al., 2017; Dann et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2018), with tight bounds scaling as O~​(H3​S​A​T)\tilde{O}(\sqrt{H^{3}SAT}). Building on this, Zanette and Brunskill (2019) provided the first variance-dependent regret bounds, introducing carefully constructed count-based bonuses that yield a highly complex algorithm and analysis. Zhou et al. (2023) recently refined this variance dependence further and established matching lower bounds, confirming the tightness of such problem-dependent results. However, both methods fundamentally require explicit uncertainty quantification through bonuses. In contrast, our algorithm achieves the same variance-dependent guarantees using a simple quantile-based ensemble mechanism—requiring no bonuses, no explicit visitation counts, and no prior knowledge of the reward distribution—while matching the lower bounds of Zhou et al. (2023).

Posterior/quantile-based exploration in MDPs. Our work also conceptually relates to Posterior Sampling for RL (PSRL) and randomized value functions (Osband et al., 2013; Agrawal and Jia, 2017; Russo, 2019). More recently, Tiapkin et al. (2022b) proposed Bayes-UCBVI, which uses quantiles of a posterior over Q-values to achieve optimal O~​(H3​S​A​T)\tilde{O}(\sqrt{H^{3}SAT}) regret without explicit bonuses. Similarly, Tiapkin et al. (2022a) take an ensembling approach using a few posterior samples. Both algorithms, however, fundamentally rely on maintaining a Dirichlet posterior over transition probabilities—an inherently count-based statistical operation—and assume the reward function is fully known. Adapting these methods to unknown reward distributions requires strong prior knowledge. Our method achieves comparable optimism using a pure data-partitioning ensemble that requires no explicit posterior computation or distributional assumptions.

Ensemble methods in bandits. Our work directly builds on Cassel et al. (2025), which introduced the batch ensemble scheme for stochastic bandits achieving variance-dependent regret without distributional assumptions. This paper is the first to extend this strictly count-free approach to MDPs. Other bandit perturbation and ensemble techniques (Lu and Van Roy, 2017; Kveton et al., 2019; Lee and Oh, 2024) or bootstrap bounds (Hao et al., 2019) either fail to adapt to unknown reward distributions, inject artificial noise, or strictly require symmetric rewards. Furthermore, while Bayesian approaches like Bayes-UCB (Kaufmann et al., 2012) use posterior quantiles, they still fundamentally rely on computing explicit count-dependent confidence levels.

Practical ensemble methods in deep RL. Ensembles are a key technique in empirical deep RL exploration. Methods such as Bootstrapped DQN (Osband et al., 2016a; Osband et al., 2016b), UCB Q-ensembles (Chen et al., 2017), Ensemble Bootstrapped Q-Learning (Peer et al., 2021), and SUNRISE (Lee et al., 2021) have demonstrated remarkable empirical success in complex environments. However, the theoretical justification for why these ensemble heuristics successfully induce exploration has remained largely open. Our work bridges this gap, providing a rigorous theoretical foundation for bonus-free ensemble-driven exploration in RL.

2 The Quantile of Means (QoM) Estimator

Standard estimators achieve optimism by explicitly subtracting an uncertainty estimate from an unbiased mean estimator. Consequently, bounding their bias requires carefully designing and computing tight uncertainty bonuses. In contrast, QoM achieves optimism purely through data partitioning and order statistics. This mechanism relies on the following corollary, which states that a minor modification to the standard sample average is optimistic with constant probability.

Corollary 2.

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} be i.i.d nonnegative random variables with expectation μ\mu. Then for any c≥1/12c\geq 1/12 it holds that: Pr⁡(∑i=1nXin+c<μ)≥1/13.\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left({\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{X_{i}}{n+c}<\mu}\right)}}\geq 1/13.

Proof.

Apply Lemma 13 in Section A.2 (Feige (2004), Theorem 1) with Xi/μX_{i}/\mu and δ=c\delta=c.

Crucially, this is not a standard concentration inequality and requires no information beyond the first moment. Using Corollary 2, the QoM estimator is optimistic if at least ⌈α​B⌉\lceil\alpha B\rceil of the subsets yield optimistic estimates. Because the BB subsets are independent, the number of optimistic subsets follows a Binomial distribution with BB trials and a success probability of at least 1/131/13. Bounding the lower tail of this Binomial variable via a Chernoff bound yields the optimism guarantee in Lemma 1.

The bias property of QoM follows a similar logic, replacing Corollary 2 with Freedman’s inequality (Lemma 14 in Section A.2). Similar guarantees can be obtained using other tail inequalities. For example, applying Chebyshev’s inequality allows us to handle unbounded random variables with finite variance, albeit with significantly worse constants. Importantly, adapting to these different distributions requires essentially no changes to the QoM estimator itself—only to the analysis. This stands in stark contrast to bonus-based estimators, where the algorithmic implementation must change to incorporate distribution-specific bonus terms.

Finally, we note that Cassel et al. (2025) recently considered the Minimum of Means estimator, which is equivalent to QoM with α=1/B\alpha=1/B. They provide similar guarantees in their Lemmas 3 and 4; however, their optimism claim is applicable only for Bernoulli or symmetric random variables, and their bias bound incurs additional logarithmic factors.

3 Setting and Notations

MDP.

A finite horizon MDP is defined by a tuple ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,H,P,ℒ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},H,P,\mathcal{L}), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a set of states (of size SS), 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a set of actions (of size AA), HH is the decision horizon, Ph,h∈[H]P_{h},h\in[H] are the transition dynamics, and ℒ\mathcal{L} is the loss distribution. Each episode k∈[K]k\in[K] starts at state s1∈𝒮s_{1}\in\mathcal{S} and proceeds inductively as follows. If at step h∈[H]h\in[H] the system is in state shk∈𝒮s_{h}^{k}\in\mathcal{S}, and an agent chooses action ahk∈𝒜a_{h}^{k}\in\mathcal{A}, then the system transitions to a new state sh+1k∈𝒮s_{h+1}^{k}\in\mathcal{S} sampled independently according to Ph(⋅∣shk,ahk)P_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{h}^{k},a_{h}^{k}), and a loss Lhk∈ℝL_{h}^{k}\in\mathbb{R} is sampled independently according to ℒh​(shk,ahk)\mathcal{L}_{h}(s_{h}^{k},a_{h}^{k}) whose mean is denoted ℓh​(shk,ahk)\ell_{h}(s_{h}^{k},a_{h}^{k}). The process ends after HH steps, at which point a new episode begins. We note that fixing the initial state is done to ease the notation and does not lose generality.

Assumption 3 (Bounded total loss).

The random losses LhL_{h} are non-negative and satisfy ∑h∈[H]Lh≤H\sum_{h\in[H]}L_{h}\leq H almost surely for all policies.

4 Algorithm and Main Result

We now introduce Value Iteration with Bootstrap Ensemble (VIBE; Algorithm 1), an algorithm that replaces explicit uncertainty bonuses with our QoM estimator. Standard optimistic algorithms construct explicit upper confidence bounds by estimating the empirical mean and subtracting a bonus proportional to the inverse square root of the visitation count. VIBE bypasses this entirely. Instead, we maintain BB independent, non-overlapping datasets 𝒟hk,b​(s,a)\mathcal{D}^{k,b}_{h}(s,a) for each state-action-step tuple.

Concretely, to ensure these datasets grow at the same rate—thereby maintaining a balanced variance across the ensemble—we assign incoming transitions (sh+1k,Lhk)(s_{h+1}^{k},L_{h}^{k}) using a strict round-robin schedule:

𝒟hk+1,b​(s,a)=𝒟hk,b​(s,a)​⋃{(sh+1k,Lhk),if ​(s,a,b)=(shk,ahk,bhk​(s,a))∅,otherwise,\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{h}^{k+1,b}(s,a)=\mathcal{D}_{h}^{k,b}(s,a)\bigcup\begin{cases}(s_{h+1}^{k},L_{h}^{k}),&\text{if }(s,a,b)=(s_{h}^{k},a_{h}^{k},b_{h}^{k}(s,a))\\ \emptyset,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (3)

where bhk​(s,a)=arg​minb∈[B]⁡\@mathmeasure\big@size1\big@size|𝒟hk,b​(s,a)\@mathmeasure\big@size1\big@size|b_{h}^{k}(s,a)=\argmin_{b\in[B]}\mathopen{\mathchoice{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 1\big@size\displaystyle\left\lvert\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 1\big@size\textstyle\left\lvert\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 0.7\big@size\scriptstyle\left\lvert\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 0.5\big@size\scriptscriptstyle\left\lvert\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}}{\mathcal{D}_{h}^{k,b}(s,a)}\mathclose{\mathchoice{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 1\big@size\displaystyle\left\rvert\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 1\big@size\textstyle\left\rvert\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 0.7\big@size\scriptstyle\left\rvert\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 0.5\big@size\scriptscriptstyle\left\rvert\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}}.

During planning, we perform standard value iteration (without bonuses), but evaluate the Q−Q-value using a QoM estimate (see Eq. 2) applied across our BB (nearly) equal non-overlapping datasets at quantile level α\alpha. Because we are minimizing loss, taking the α\alpha-quantile of the QQ-value estimates naturally filters out overestimations while implicitly establishing a high-probability optimistic lower bound on the true loss-to-go. The full procedure is detailed in Algorithm 1.

From a practical standpoint, VIBE is highly tunable. It requires only two hyperparameters: the quantile level α\alpha (which is constant) and the number of batches BB (which scales logarithmically with H,S,KH,S,K, and δ−1\delta^{-1}). Computationally, VIBE essentially runs value iteration BB times per episode, taking O⁡(S​A​H​B)O(SAHB) time. Because BB is logarithmic, this ensemble approach introduces negligible overhead compared to standard bonus-based value iteration.

Main result.

To state our theoretical guarantees, we characterize the problem complexity using the maximum cumulative conditional variance of the MDP, similarly to Zanette and Brunskill (2019). We define ℚ⋆=∑h∈[H]ℚh⋆\mathbb{Q}^{\star}=\sum_{h\in[H]}\mathbb{Q}_{h}^{\star} where

ℚh⋆=maxs∈𝒮,a∈A⁡Vars,a,h(Lh+Vh+1⋆​(sh+1)).\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}_{h}^{\star}=\max_{s\in\mathcal{S},a\in A}\Var_{s,a,h}(L_{h}+V_{h+1}^{\star}(s_{h+1})). (4)

Theorem 4 establishes that VIBE achieves a variance-dependent regret bound without requiring explicit variance estimation or bonuses. See proof in Section 6, and discussion on extending to heavy-tailed losses in Appendix B.

(2023).

5 Ensembles as a Tool for Optimism

Having established VIBE’s theoretical guarantees and algorithmic simplicity, we now dissect the mathematical engine driving these results. The purpose of this section is to formally demonstrate how our ensemble quantile mechanism naturally induces optimism in the MDP setting, bypassing the need for explicit uncertainty bonuses. To see this, we first decompose the cumulative regret into two standard components—colloquially referred to as bias and optimism:

regretK=∑k∈[K]V1πk​(s1)−V^1k​(s1)⏟bias+∑k∈[K]V^1k​(s1)−V1⋆​(s1)⏟optimism.\displaystyle\mathrm{regret}_{K}=\sum_{k\in[K]}\underbrace{V_{1}^{\pi^{k}}(s_{1})-\hat{V}_{1}^{k}(s_{1})}_{\text{bias}}+\sum_{k\in[K]}\underbrace{\hat{V}_{1}^{k}(s_{1})-V_{1}^{\star}(s_{1})}_{\text{optimism}}. (5)

The primary goal of optimistic algorithms is to ensure that the optimism term is non-positive , and thus the total regret is bounded entirely by the bias term. Traditionally, bounding the optimism term requires carefully designed count-based bonuses, which then become the dominant factor when analyzing the bias. Because VIBE completely forgoes explicit bonuses, the analysis of our bias term is significantly simplified and relies mostly on standard techniques (detailed in Section 6.1). In what follows, we show that our QoM approach achieves optimism on the following high-probability event.

6 Regret Analysis

As established in Section 5, our ensemble approach ensures the optimism term in the regret decomposition is non-positive. Consequently, the regret of VIBE is bounded entirely by the bias. To formalize this, we first define our empirical counters and operators. ∑k∈[K]𝔼πk,P∑h∈[H]\displaystyle\sum_{k\in[K]}\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{k},P}\sum_{h\in[H]} βhk​(sh,ah)≤2​B​H​S​A​κ.\displaystyle\beta_{h}^{k}(s_{h},a_{h})\leq 2BHSA\kappa. (10)

These conditions capture the essential statistical properties needed to bound the regret. Equation (6) establishes optimism, ensuring the QoM estimator does not overestimate the loss of the optimal action. Equation (7) bounds the algorithm’s bias by limiting how much the estimator can underestimate the true Bellman target for any action. Equations (8) and (9) ensure the empirical transition probabilities concentrate around the true dynamics. Notice that the error here scales multiplicatively with the true transition probabilities, which is a strict requirement for achieving variance-dependent bounds. Finally, Equation (10) bounds the cumulative sum of the statistical errors (the inverse counts) encountered by the agent across all episodes.

The following two lemmas establish that ℰ\mathcal{E} holds with high probability, and that under ℰ\mathcal{E}, the cumulative bias is bounded by the problem’s structural variance (proofs in Sections 6.1 and 6.2).

Lemma 7 (Good Event).

Appendix A Additional Proofs

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1 (QoM)

For the first part, notice that the event holds when at least ⌈α​B⌉\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil{\alpha B}\right\rceil}} batches yield an estimate less than or equal to μ\mu. By Corollary 2, each batch satisfies this with probability at least 1/131/13. Because the subsets 𝒟b\mathcal{D}^{b} are fixed and disjoint, they are independent. Letting Bin⁡(n,p)\mathrm{Bin}(n,p) be the binomial distribution with nn trails and success probability pp, we conclude that

Pr⁡(μ^α≤μ)≥Pr⁡(Bin⁡(B,1/13)≥⌈B/65⌉)\displaystyle\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left({\hat{\mu}_{\alpha}\leq\mu}\right)}}\geq\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left({\mathrm{Bin}(B,1/13)\geq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lceil{B/65}\right\rceil}}}\right)}} ≥Pr⁡(Bin⁡(B,1/13)>B/65)\displaystyle\geq\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left({\mathrm{Bin}(B,1/13)>B/65}\right)}}
=1−Pr⁡(Bin⁡(B,1/13)≤B/65)\displaystyle=1-\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left({\mathrm{Bin}(B,1/13)\leq B/65}\right)}}
≥1−exp(−B⋅DKL(1/65||1/13))\displaystyle\geq 1-\exp(-B\cdot\mathrm{D_{KL}}(1/65||1/13))
≥1−exp(−B/26)\displaystyle\geq 1-\exp(-B/26)
≥1−δ,\displaystyle\geq 1-\delta,

where the fourth transition used a standard Chernoff bound for Binomial random variables, and DKL\mathrm{D_{KL}} is the Kullback–Leibler divergence.

A.2.2 Variance Manipulation

The following result is a variant of Lemma 21 in Merlis [2024].

Lemma 10.

Let V,V¯,V¯∈[0,H]𝒮V,\overline{V},\underline{V}\in[0,H]^{\mathcal{S}} be value functions such that V¯​(s)≤V⁡(s)≤V¯​(s)\underline{V}(s)\leq V(s)\leq\overline{V}(s) for all s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}. Then for any h∈[H],s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜,β,η>0h\in[H],s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A},\beta,\eta>0

β​Vars,a,h(Lh+V⁡(sh+1))≤η−1​Vars,a,h(Lh+V¯​(sh+1))+13​H​Ph​(V¯−V¯)​(sh,ah)+(3​H2+η)​β4.\displaystyle\sqrt{\beta\Var_{s,a,h}(L_{h}+V(s_{h+1}))}\leq\eta^{-1}\Var_{s,a,h}(L_{h}+\overline{V}(s_{h+1}))+\frac{1}{3H}P_{h}(\overline{{V}}-\underline{V})(s_{h},a_{h})+\frac{(3H^{2}+\eta)\beta}{4}.
Proof.

Recall that the standard deviation satisfies a triangle inequality (see Zanette and Brunskill [2019] Eqs. 48-51), i.e., for σ⁡(X)=Var(X)\sigma(X)=\sqrt{\Var(X)} we have σ⁡(X+Y)≤σ⁡(X)+σ⁡(Y)\sigma(X+Y)\leq\sigma(X)+\sigma(Y). Thus, we have

β​Vars,a,h(Lh+V⁡(sh+1))≤β​Vars,a,h(Lh+V¯​(sh+1))+β​Vars,a,h((V−V¯)​(sh+1)).\displaystyle\sqrt{\beta\Var_{s,a,h}(L_{h}+V(s_{h+1}))}\leq\sqrt{\beta\Var_{s,a,h}(L_{h}+\overline{V}(s_{h+1}))}+\sqrt{\beta\Var_{s,a,h}((V-\overline{V})(s_{h+1}))}.

Now, using our assumption on the value functions, we have

β​Vars,a,h((V−V¯)​(sh+1))≤β​H​Ph​(V¯−V)​(s,a)\displaystyle\sqrt{\beta\Var_{s,a,h}((V-\overline{V})(s_{h+1}))}\leq\sqrt{\beta HP_{h}(\overline{V}-V)(s,a)} ≤β​H​Ph​(V¯−V¯)​(s,a)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\beta HP_{h}(\overline{V}-\underline{V})(s,a)}
≤(1/3​H)​Ph​(V¯−V¯)​(s,a)+(3/4)​H2​β,\displaystyle\leq(1/3H)P_{h}(\overline{V}-\underline{V})(s,a)+(3/4)H^{2}\beta,

where the last step also used the AM-GM inequality (a​b≤(a2+b2)/2\sqrt{ab}\leq(a^{2}+b^{2})/2). Plugging this into the previous inequality and using AM-GM on the first term concludes the proof.

Next, we state the well-known Law of Total Variance (LTV), originally due to Azar et al. [2017].

Lemma 11 (Zanette and Brunskill [2019], Lemma 15).

For any policy π\pi, it holds that

𝔼P,π​[∑h∈[H]Varsh,ah,h(Vπ​(sh+1))]=𝔼P,π​[∑h∈[H]ℓh​(sh,ah)−V1π​(s1)]2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{P,\pi}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[{\sum_{h\in[H]}\Var_{s_{h},a_{h},h}(V^{\pi}(s_{h+1}))}\right]}}=\mathbb{E}_{P,\pi}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[{\sum_{h\in[H]}\ell_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-V_{1}^{\pi}(s_{1})}\right]}}^{2}
Lemma 12 (Variance Bound).

For any policy π:𝒮→𝒜\pi:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A} we have

𝔼P,π​∑h∈[H]Varsh,ah,h(Lh+Vh+1π​(sh+1))=𝔼P,π,L​[∑h∈[H]Lh−V1π​(s1)]2≤H​V1π​(s1).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{P,\pi}\sum_{h\in[H]}\Var_{s_{h},a_{h},h}(L_{h}+V_{h+1}^{\pi}(s_{h+1}))=\mathbb{E}_{P,\pi,L}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[{\sum_{h\in[H]}L_{h}-V_{1}^{\pi}(s_{1})}\right]}}^{2}\leq HV_{1}^{\pi}(s_{1}).

Furthermore, conditioned on ι\iota, the losses are independent, thus 𝔼P,π​∑h∈[H]Varsh,ah,h(Lh)=𝔼P,π,L​(∑h∈[H]Lh−ℓh​(sh,ah))2\mathbb{E}_{P,\pi}\sum_{h\in[H]}\Var_{s_{h},a_{h},h}(L_{h})=\mathbb{E}_{P,\pi,L}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left({\sum_{h\in[H]}L_{h}-\ell_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})}\right)}}^{2} . A.2.3 Statistical Inequalities

Lemma 13 (Feige [2004], Theorem 1).

Appendix B Extension to Heavy-Tailed Losses

In this section we discuss how Theorem 4 extends to losses with heavy tails. Specifically, we can replace Assumption 3 with the weaker requirement that the random losses LhL_{h} are non-negative, satisfy 𝔼​[∑h∈[H]Lh]≤H\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[{\sum_{h\in[H]}L_{h}}\right]}}\leq H for all policies, and each Lh​(s,a)L_{h}(s,a) has finite (but unknown) variance.

The key observation enabling this extension is that Lemma 1 applies to non-negative random variables with finite variance, without requiring boundedness (as discussed following its statement). Consequently, the QoM estimator remains optimistic and its bias increases by at most a constant multiplicative factor in this setting. Given this, the good event used in the proof of Theorem 4 holds essentially unchanged, and the remainder of the regret decomposition follows straightforwardly, yielding the same regret bound up to constants.

We note, however, that the min\@mathmeasure\big@size1\big@size{ℚ⋆,HV⋆\@mathmeasure\big@size1\big@size}\min\mathopen{\mathchoice{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 1\big@size\displaystyle\left\{\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 1\big@size\textstyle\left\{\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 0.7\big@size\scriptstyle\left\{\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 0.5\big@size\scriptscriptstyle\left\{\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}}{\mathbb{Q}^{\star},HV^{\star}}\mathclose{\mathchoice{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 1\big@size\displaystyle\left\}\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 1\big@size\textstyle\left\}\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 0.7\big@size\scriptstyle\left\}\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}{{\@mathmeasure{}{\big@size 0.5\big@size\scriptscriptstyle\left\}\vbox to0.0pt{}\right.}}}} term appearing in Theorem 4 reduces to ℚ⋆\mathbb{Q}^{\star} alone in the heavy-tailed setting. The H​V⋆HV^{\star} term arises from bounding the variance of the value function under the optimal policy, which relies on the losses being almost surely bounded. Since no such bound is assumed in the heavy-tailed setting, this refinement does not apply, and we cannot expect the H​V⋆HV^{\star} term to appear in the regret bound.

Appendix C Multi-Armed Bandits

Problem setup.

A stochastic multi-armed bandit is an MDP with a single state and horizon one, i.e., S=H=1S=H=1 (see Section 3). Thus, we simplify the notation as follows. In each episode, k∈[K]k\in[K] the agent chooses an arm ak∈𝒜a^{k}\in\mathcal{A} and observes a stochastic loss Lk∈[0,1]L^{k}\in[0,1] sampled independently from a distribution ℒ⁡(ak)\mathcal{L}(a^{k}) whose mean and variance are denoted ℓ⁡(ak),σ2​(ak)\ell(a^{k}),\sigma^{2}(a^{k}). Denoting the optimal action and value as a⋆∈arg​mina∈𝒜⁡ℓ​(a)a^{\star}\in\argmin_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\ell(a) and ℓ⋆=μ⁡(a⋆)\ell^{\star}=\mu(a^{\star}), the (pseudo) regret can be rewritten as

regretK=∑k∈[K][ℓ⁡(ak)−ℓ⋆]=∑k∈[K]Δ⁡(ak),\displaystyle\mathrm{regret}_{K}=\sum_{k\in[K]}[\ell(a^{k})-\ell^{\star}]=\sum_{k\in[K]}\Delta(a^{k}),

where Δ⁡(a)=ℓ⁡(a)−ℓ⋆\Delta(a)=\ell(a)-\ell^{\star} is known as the sub-optimality gap of arm a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}.

C.1 Algorithm and Main Results

We present Algorithm 2, which is identical to Algorithm 1 but with a simplified notation.

The following is our main result for multi-armed bandits (proof in Section C.2).

Suppose we run Algorithm 2 with number of batches B=26​log⁡(2​K​A​δ−1)B=26\log(2KA\delta^{-1}), and quantile level α=1/65\alpha=1/65. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the following hold simultaneously

regretK\displaystyle\mathrm{regret}_{K} ≤76​K​∑a≠a⋆σ2​(a)​log⁡(6​K​A​δ−1)+469​A​log⁡(2​K​A​δ−1)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{76K\sum_{a\neq a^{\star}}\sigma^{2}(a)\log(6KA\delta^{-1})}+469A\log(2KA\delta^{-1})
regretK\displaystyle\mathrm{regret}_{K} ≤∑a≠a⋆(76​σ2​(a)Δ⁡(a)+469)​log⁡(2​K​A​δ−1).\displaystyle\leq\sum_{a\neq a^{\star}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left({\frac{76\sigma^{2}(a)}{\Delta(a)}+469}\right)}}\log(2KA\delta^{-1}).

We note that Feige [2004] conjecture that their result, stated here as Lemma 13, holds with a constant of 1/e1/e. If true, this would change the numerical constant in the batch size to 5.55.5, and a better choice of α\alpha would be 1/101/10. Overall, this would decrease the constants in our bounds. Finally, we note that this result does not require the losses to be bounded in [0,1][0,1]. In fact, it holds even for nonnegative losses with finite variance, albeit with significantly larger numerical constants. To see this, replace the use of Freedman’s inequality in the proof of Lemma 1 with Chebyshev’s inequality.
